The Triassic Period. Lasting from two hundred and fifty-two to two hundred and one million years ago, the Triassic marks the recovery from the Permian extinction and the rise of dinosaurs. Named for its three distinctive rock layers—tri-assic—the Triassic saw reptiles inherit the barren landscape left by the Great Dying. Mammals emerged as small, shrew-like creatures during this era. Pangaea slowly began to rift apart.

Dinosaurs first appeared in the early Triassic and diversified steadily, beginning as bipedal predators like Eoraptor. The synapsids and therapsids were decimated by the Permian extinction, and their survivors evolved into early mammals, which remained small and nocturnal throughout this period. Archosaurs, the clade that includes dinosaurs and crocodilians, rose to dominance, with early forms like Lagosuchus anticipating dinosaurian body plans.

Conifers and cycads became the dominant plants during the Triassic, as flowering plants had not yet evolved. Marine reptiles like ichthyosaurs, fish-like predators, and nothosaurs colonised the recovering oceans. The Triassic extinction struck around two hundred and one million years ago, clearing the way for dinosaurs to become Earth's dominant vertebrates.

This period follows the catastrophic Permian extinction, which allowed the Triassic recovery, and precedes the Jurassic Period, when dinosaurs reached their peak, with dinosaurs themselves representing the dominant vertebrates that rose during the Triassic.
